Editorial note: This English edition preserves the historical article’s prose and research statement. Product capabilities, rankings, model releases, institutional citations and methodology-performance claims are attributed to the November 2025 source, not independently verified current facts. The geographic categories distinguish Chinese heritage from Chinese nationality as defined by the source. Its definitions of unique visitors and subscription revenue labeled ARR are reproduced as its own definitions, not substituted for standard analytics or annualized recurring-revenue definitions. The prose uses rounded totals and growth multiples; they must not be interpreted as exact measurements or percentage-point changes. Monthly active users are reported across products, not established here as a deduplicated count of people. The source’s title wording “ChatGPT-5.1” and product groupings are retained.

Today, many people opening ChatGPT will find two new names in the model list: GPT-5.1 Instant and GPT-5.1 Thinking. OpenAI says officially that they are more conversational, follow instructions better, and can automatically decide whether to spend more time thinking based on a question's difficulty.

Go back a few weeks and October was packed with AI news: the Sora 2 upgrade, the launch of the Atlas browser, and a succession of new models. From hyperrealistic video and AI browsers to small multimodal models, everyone was competing for the next-generation gateway.

But from the user's perspective, there is a more straightforward question:

however powerful the models become, what actually gets opened every day? Who is truly capturing the real traffic from this wave of intelligence?

That is what our October 2025 AI Web Application Top Ranking seeks to answer:

not who has the most parameters, but who is typed most often into the browser's address bar.

I. Concentration at the top is approaching imbalance

Start with the most intuitive figure.

Across the global AI Web Top 100 we tracked, total October visits were approximately 10.61 billion. Of those:

ChatGPT alone captured approximately 58.1% of traffic;

the Top 10 together took 82.6%;

and the Top 50 accounted for 95.4%.

Looking more closely:

ChatGPT recorded approximately 6.17 billion Web visits in October.

By active users, monthly MAU across global AI Web applications reached approximately 1.51 billion, with ChatGPT accounting for about 32%.

In other words, for many ordinary users, the concrete browser experience of “using AI” can almost be equated with opening ChatGPT.

That has two implications for newcomers:

the difficulty of building another general-purpose gateway is now extreme. You are not competing with a product but with an established cognitive habit—an action akin to “Baidu it” or “Google it.”

Yet it also means that any gateway able to capture even one specific scenario—even 1% of users' time—represents an enormous opportunity. When leading applications handle general conversation, users become more willing to assign certain fixed tasks to specialized products.

II. Category distribution: chatbots take three quarters, but four major branches have truly formed

When the 10.61 billion visits are viewed by functional category, the conclusion is equally blunt: chatbots account for approximately 75.8% of Web traffic. They are followed by emotional companionship at about 4.1%, intelligent search at about 3.7%, personal assistants at about 3.6%, and then image editing, image generation, education, video generation, knowledge management, and other categories, each at roughly 1%–1.5%.

You can think of it as a tree:

the trunk is conversational chat. Whether ChatGPT, Gemini, deepseek, or Copilot, products are still developing around the fundamental interaction paradigm of conversation.

Several thick branches grow upward:

Emotional companionship: Character.AI, CrushOn, and others take “talking with you” to its extreme;

Intelligent search: Perplexity and others rewrite the search experience;

Content creation—images, text, and video: only after those come large-scale image generation, video generation, writing, PPT, and other tools.

This also answers a frequently asked question: will AI quickly wipe out every vertical tool?

Data from October suggests an answer closer to this: general-purpose foundation models consume the gateway, but they do not consume the task.

Whether users reserve a browser tab for an independent website depends on whether it makes a particular task noticeably easier, faster, or more fun.

III. Chinese applications: only 8% of traffic, but the story lies in the structure

Within the global Top 100, we classify both domestic-market and outbound products as Chinese applications. Combining them shows that:

the Chinese cohort—domestic + outbound—captured approximately 7.9% of Web traffic in the global Top 100;

looking only at products labeled domestic, traffic serving exclusively the Chinese market accounted for about 5.8%;

outbound products contributed approximately 2.0% of traffic in the global ranking.

At first glance, 7.9% is not dazzling, but its structure is extremely interesting.

1. Domestic: deepseek is the undisputed star player on the home server

In the domestic AI Web Top 100 that we track separately, October traffic totaled approximately 720 million visits. Of that:

deepseek alone accounted for approximately 47.4% of domestic Web traffic;

the Top five—deepseek, Doubao, Quark, Baidu AI Search, and Kimi—together took 81.9%.

In other words, within the browser world of Chinese users, chatting with/searching via AI in Chinese is increasingly being handled by these few products:

deepseek ranks No. 3 in the global ranking and also leads both domestic Web traffic and domestic MAU;

it contributes roughly 3.2% of total visits in the global Top 100,

while in the domestic Top 100 it accounts for nearly half of traffic + approximately 29% of domestic Web MAU.

Quark + Baidu AI Search + Doubao + Kimi play roles in China that are closer to established gateways extended with AI.

In growth terms, approximately 69% of products in the global Top 100 posted positive month-on-month visits, with median traffic growth of about 3.8%;

in the domestic Top 100, however, that fell to approximately 45% of products still growing month on month, with median traffic growth at -2.1%—a modest overall contraction.

Two things are happening at the same time:

Chinese users' preferred AI sites are consolidating, and the leading players are becoming more entrenched;

it is becoming rapidly more difficult for mid-tier products to compete for attention, especially those that have not established differentiation and are not supported by a must-have use case.

2. Outbound: Chinese teams have developed a different persona overseas

Now consider that 2% of outbound traffic.

Among the global Top 100, the 14 products labeled outbound together received approximately 2.0% of traffic. If we view them as a small universe of their own, it looks entirely different from the domestic universe:

within outbound traffic, image generation accounts for approximately 27.3%, emotional companionship for approximately 24.1%, and chatbots for only 15.0%.

In other words, the Chinese teams that have truly established themselves overseas look more like these categories:

AI art communities/asset platforms such as SeaArt, PixAI.Art, and TensorArt;

products such as PolyBuzz and CrushOn.AI that focus on emotional companionship and emotional value;

plus Qwen, Monica, Genspark, and others that have found specific entry points between chat and search. A pattern emerges: successful outbound products are not “overseas versions of ChatGPT”; they go deep on one particular desire/need.

Some capture the supply advantage of images that are good enough and cheap enough; others exploit cultural openings around emotional companionship + role-playing. These are areas that local giants cannot yet prioritize or may find inconvenient to enter aggressively at scale.

The real dark horses are not those that speak better, but those that grow faster at a task. The growth rankings are always the most interesting. Creati, which integrated the Sora 2 and Veo 3.1 models, ranked first, with month-on-month growth surging 14.8-fold and corresponding active users rising 28.5-fold. The names at the very front of the global growth ranking are almost all task-oriented products.

Place them together and a simple but important principle appears:

in the GPT-5 era, the more a product resembles a dedicated tool, the more likely it is to leave its name on the growth rankings;

the more it resembles yet another all-purpose gateway, the more likely it is to remain in the shadow of the dominant giants.

3. Domestic dark horses: the Minimax ecosystem, WPS AI, and Pic Copilot capture both in-house demand and small consumer pleasures

On the domestic side, the story in the growth rankings is different again.

In the domestic visits-growth ranking, several types of contender appear:

Tunee AI ranks first, as music generation also surges in China;

MiniMax Open Platform + MiniMax Agent:

the former is a model-training/platform gateway for developers and enterprises, while the latter is a To C intelligent-search product. Both rank highly in visits and active-user growth, showing that a strategy combining platform and application has begun to form its own flywheel in China.

WPS AI: as the AI module of established office software, its visits grew more than 60% month on month;

Pic Copilot, Jianpian, Luban, and other Alibaba-affiliated image-editing/design tools posted steady growth, continuing to validate demand for AI to “handle images for you” in e-commerce operations, design-assistant work, and related scenarios.

Viewed through the domestic active-user growth ranking, the pattern becomes even clearer:

Tunee AI, MiniMax Open Platform, and MiniMax Agent remain near the front;

Baidu Comate (coding assistant), Huixiang (video generation), Immersive Translate, and other tools also fall within the 30%–50% MAU growth range.

These products share two characteristics:

they do not seek to replace ChatGPT, but anchor themselves in a fixed scenario with very high repeat frequency;

they do not build a new website for you to sample, but embed themselves in the toolchain you already use: browser bookmarks, office software, browser extensions, and team workflows.

IV. Watch behavioral changes in the browser, not just model versions

What will the launch of GPT-5.1 bring?

For most end-user Web products, it may mean:

a better general-purpose conversational experience;

continued increases in users' expectations of AI answers;

and general questions being handled more readily by system-level gateways.

Yet our October ranking suggests that these changes deserve closer attention:

for which scenarios are users willing to open one more independent browser tab?

Is it to translate better, edit a clip faster, or let an Agent complete routine tasks?

Which behaviors have moved from “is this fun to try?” to “I cannot do without it”?

For example, some creators have already formed the habit of opening Creati / Tunee every day,

while some programmers are deeply tied to Comate / Toolhouse within their company's unified toolchain. Model upgrades are productivity infrastructure; the distribution of Web traffic is the real vote in this round of AI competition.

This October 2025 AI Web dataset cannot tell you what the landscape will look like three years from now.

It can tell you how users are actually behaving in their browsers right now:

whom they trust, whom they depend on, and for which small task they will deliberately open another webpage.

If I hide the model names and look only at browser-tab histories, does my product have a presence?

If the answer is still no, that is all right.

After all, a model can be upgraded overnight,

but a webpage worth opening every day is always worth crafting patiently.

02. Research Statement

2.1 Data Notes

AI-product revenue figures in this report, article, ranking, or chart are based on real-time tracking of traffic from AI product websites to payment gateways such as Stripe, combined with time-series analysis of historical visits, monthly-active-user fluctuations, and changes in pricing strategies to build a dynamic revenue-estimation model. The model's core parameters are determined through a three-part validation system covering paid-conversion-funnel monitoring, reverse calibration against corporate disclosures, and comparison with industry benchmark conversion rates, and are promptly compared with and corrected against company financial reports, financing announcements, and disclosures from authoritative media. In sampling validation, the mean absolute error rate between estimates and actual data remained within ±10%, meeting the standard for industry-grade research.

AI-product traffic figures in this report, article, ranking, or chart are derived from multisource data integration and processing by Unique Research's proprietary algorithms. Monitoring is strictly limited to direct user access through official applications and websites. Specifically, the data covers only direct user visits to AI products through websites and native applications. It excludes traffic generated through browser plugins/extensions, desktop software clients, WeChat/Alipay mini-program ecosystems, embedded services on third-party platforms such as Discord, local deployment of open-source models, API calls, and other indirect-access scenarios. The data focuses on direct access to the core endpoints of AI products in order to objectively reflect direct usage behavior on mainstream user devices.

Given the complexity and dynamism of data collection and processing, as well as constant changes in the market environment, the displayed data may contain some errors and omissions. It should therefore be regarded as a research and analytical reference that offers a window into AI product markets, rather than definitive evidence for a specific investment strategy or consulting recommendation.

2.2 Concept Definitions

• Geographic dimension

Overseas AI products: products founded by entrepreneurs or teams not of Chinese heritage and launched primarily for global markets, including but not limited to their home markets.

Domestic AI products: products founded by Chinese-national entrepreneurs or teams and launched primarily for China's domestic market.

Outbound AI products: products founded by entrepreneurs or teams of Chinese heritage but whose primary target markets are overseas, outside mainland China.

• Functional dimension

AI-native applications: applications designed from inception around deep integration of artificial-intelligence technologies and algorithms, whose core value, business processes, or user experience depend entirely on AI. They do not merely use AI to optimize or enhance existing functions; AI is their core component, and without it these applications would cease to exist or lose their fundamental value.

AI-enabled applications: applications that integrate or embed AI into an existing business logic and application framework to enhance current functions or provide entirely new ones. These applications may already have had mature business models and market positioning, but introducing AI can significantly improve efficiency and user experience or create new value.

AI-ecosystem applications: platforms that support, connect, or facilitate exchange among AI technology researchers, application developers, service providers, end users, and others in the AI ecosystem. These applications extend beyond technology to markets, communities, resource sharing, and other dimensions, with the aim of advancing adoption, innovation, and collaboration in AI.

2.3 Metric Definitions

• WEB data metrics

Visits: the total number of visits to a website during a specified period, such as one month, used to measure traffic scale. Pageviews during a continuous active period count as the same session; renewed activity after an interval of more than 30 minutes, or activity beginning on a new day, is counted as a new visit, providing a comprehensive and precise measure of traffic and visitor activity.

Unique Visitors: the number of distinct IP addresses that visit the target website during a specified period, such as one month. If someone visits a website on multiple days within one month, that person is counted only once.

Subscription revenue (labeled ARR in the source): all revenue earned over a given period, such as one year, from subscription services provided by the website, excluding one-off sources such as advertising revenue, transaction commissions, and professional services.

• APP data metrics

Downloads: the number of times an App is downloaded during a specified period, such as one month, generally measured as the number of downloads of an individual App from stores such as the App Store and Google Play. Downloads measure an App's popularity and ability to attract users and can also reflect the effectiveness of promotion and marketing.

Active Users: the number of distinct users who performed at least one activity during a specified period, such as one month. Active users measure user scale and engagement during a given period.

In-app purchases (IAP): revenue generated when users buy virtual goods, additional services, premium features, and other items inside an App. This excludes advertising revenue, direct user payments such as tips, and third-party Android app stores.

Appendix: Summary of Quarterly Trend Insights

At the top layer is the entrenchment of gateways. The general conversational gateway represented by ChatGPT has become the global default, while the Chinese market is rapidly consolidating around deepseek, Doubao, Quark, Baidu AI Search, Kimi, and a few others. Users are not looking for the next ChatGPT; they are committing their limited attention to a very small number of brands. This means that the barrier to creating another general-purpose gateway at the level of a browser start page has shifted from a technology problem to one of recognition and habit.

The middle layer is the distribution of tasks. From Creati and Tunee to Toolhouse and Supermemory AI, and then to WPS AI, AI image tools, and translation tools in China, the fastest-growing products share one trait: they do not try to do everything, but make one concrete task something users cannot do without. Once general-purpose models such as GPT-5.1 become infrastructure, real incremental value comes from whoever can better handle a high-frequency action—editing a video, adding music, writing a document, or running an automated workflow.

The bottom layer is the flowering of use cases. In China, Chinese teams are competing more heavily for the default gateway to the Chinese-language world; overseas, they have produced products with an entirely different character. Outbound applications built around AI art, emotional companionship, and creator communities capture narrow openings in culture and demand rather than competing with global giants on parameters and models. Beneath the modest contraction in domestic traffic is the rapid concentration of user behavior around a few leaders and clear use cases; the small universe represented by that 2% outbound share proves that focusing on one scenario and telling its story well can still open a path into the global rankings.

If the AI Web trend in October had to be summarized in one sentence, it would be this: models are becoming homogeneous and gateways are solidifying, yet users' specific tasks, emotions, and habits are continually being reinvented. What is really worth pursuing is not the next giant gateway, but the small use case for which users quietly open one more browser tab every day.

Editorial note: This English edition preserves the historical article’s prose and research statement. Product capabilities, rankings, model releases, institutional citations and methodology-performance claims are attributed to the November 2025 source, not independently verified current facts. The geographic categories distinguish Chinese heritage from Chinese nationality as defined by the source. Its definitions of unique visitors and subscription revenue labeled ARR are reproduced as its own definitions, not substituted for standard analytics or annualized recurring-revenue definitions. The prose uses rounded totals and growth multiples; they must not be interpreted as exact measurements or percentage-point changes. Monthly active users are reported across products, not established here as a deduplicated count of people. The source’s title wording “ChatGPT-5.1” and product groupings are retained.

Today, many people opening ChatGPT will find two new names in the model list: GPT-5.1 Instant and GPT-5.1 Thinking. OpenAI says officially that they are more conversational, follow instructions better, and can automatically decide whether to spend more time thinking based on a question's difficulty.

Go back a few weeks and October was packed with AI news: the Sora 2 upgrade, the launch of the Atlas browser, and a succession of new models. From hyperrealistic video and AI browsers to small multimodal models, everyone was competing for the next-generation gateway.

But from the user's perspective, there is a more straightforward question:

however powerful the models become, what actually gets opened every day? Who is truly capturing the real traffic from this wave of intelligence?

That is what our October 2025 AI Web Application Top Ranking seeks to answer:

not who has the most parameters, but who is typed most often into the browser's address bar.

I. Concentration at the top is approaching imbalance

Start with the most intuitive figure.

Across the global AI Web Top 100 we tracked, total October visits were approximately 10.61 billion. Of those:

ChatGPT alone captured approximately 58.1% of traffic;

the Top 10 together took 82.6%;

and the Top 50 accounted for 95.4%.

Looking more closely:

ChatGPT recorded approximately 6.17 billion Web visits in October.

By active users, monthly MAU across global AI Web applications reached approximately 1.51 billion, with ChatGPT accounting for about 32%.

In other words, for many ordinary users, the concrete browser experience of “using AI” can almost be equated with opening ChatGPT.

That has two implications for newcomers:

the difficulty of building another general-purpose gateway is now extreme. You are not competing with a product but with an established cognitive habit—an action akin to “Baidu it” or “Google it.”

Yet it also means that any gateway able to capture even one specific scenario—even 1% of users' time—represents an enormous opportunity. When leading applications handle general conversation, users become more willing to assign certain fixed tasks to specialized products.

II. Category distribution: chatbots take three quarters, but four major branches have truly formed

When the 10.61 billion visits are viewed by functional category, the conclusion is equally blunt: chatbots account for approximately 75.8% of Web traffic. They are followed by emotional companionship at about 4.1%, intelligent search at about 3.7%, personal assistants at about 3.6%, and then image editing, image generation, education, video generation, knowledge management, and other categories, each at roughly 1%–1.5%.

You can think of it as a tree:

the trunk is conversational chat. Whether ChatGPT, Gemini, deepseek, or Copilot, products are still developing around the fundamental interaction paradigm of conversation.

Several thick branches grow upward:

Emotional companionship: Character.AI, CrushOn, and others take “talking with you” to its extreme;

Intelligent search: Perplexity and others rewrite the search experience;

Content creation—images, text, and video: only after those come large-scale image generation, video generation, writing, PPT, and other tools.

This also answers a frequently asked question: will AI quickly wipe out every vertical tool?

Data from October suggests an answer closer to this: general-purpose foundation models consume the gateway, but they do not consume the task.

Whether users reserve a browser tab for an independent website depends on whether it makes a particular task noticeably easier, faster, or more fun.

III. Chinese applications: only 8% of traffic, but the story lies in the structure

Within the global Top 100, we classify both domestic-market and outbound products as Chinese applications. Combining them shows that:

the Chinese cohort—domestic + outbound—captured approximately 7.9% of Web traffic in the global Top 100;

looking only at products labeled domestic, traffic serving exclusively the Chinese market accounted for about 5.8%;

outbound products contributed approximately 2.0% of traffic in the global ranking.

At first glance, 7.9% is not dazzling, but its structure is extremely interesting.

1. Domestic: deepseek is the undisputed star player on the home server

In the domestic AI Web Top 100 that we track separately, October traffic totaled approximately 720 million visits. Of that:

deepseek alone accounted for approximately 47.4% of domestic Web traffic;

the Top five—deepseek, Doubao, Quark, Baidu AI Search, and Kimi—together took 81.9%.

In other words, within the browser world of Chinese users, chatting with/searching via AI in Chinese is increasingly being handled by these few products:

deepseek ranks No. 3 in the global ranking and also leads both domestic Web traffic and domestic MAU;

it contributes roughly 3.2% of total visits in the global Top 100,

while in the domestic Top 100 it accounts for nearly half of traffic + approximately 29% of domestic Web MAU.

Quark + Baidu AI Search + Doubao + Kimi play roles in China that are closer to established gateways extended with AI.

In growth terms, approximately 69% of products in the global Top 100 posted positive month-on-month visits, with median traffic growth of about 3.8%;

in the domestic Top 100, however, that fell to approximately 45% of products still growing month on month, with median traffic growth at -2.1%—a modest overall contraction.

Two things are happening at the same time:

Chinese users' preferred AI sites are consolidating, and the leading players are becoming more entrenched;

it is becoming rapidly more difficult for mid-tier products to compete for attention, especially those that have not established differentiation and are not supported by a must-have use case.

2. Outbound: Chinese teams have developed a different persona overseas

Now consider that 2% of outbound traffic.

Among the global Top 100, the 14 products labeled outbound together received approximately 2.0% of traffic. If we view them as a small universe of their own, it looks entirely different from the domestic universe:

within outbound traffic, image generation accounts for approximately 27.3%, emotional companionship for approximately 24.1%, and chatbots for only 15.0%.

In other words, the Chinese teams that have truly established themselves overseas look more like these categories:

AI art communities/asset platforms such as SeaArt, PixAI.Art, and TensorArt;

products such as PolyBuzz and CrushOn.AI that focus on emotional companionship and emotional value;

plus Qwen, Monica, Genspark, and others that have found specific entry points between chat and search. A pattern emerges: successful outbound products are not “overseas versions of ChatGPT”; they go deep on one particular desire/need.

Some capture the supply advantage of images that are good enough and cheap enough; others exploit cultural openings around emotional companionship + role-playing. These are areas that local giants cannot yet prioritize or may find inconvenient to enter aggressively at scale.

The real dark horses are not those that speak better, but those that grow faster at a task. The growth rankings are always the most interesting. Creati, which integrated the Sora 2 and Veo 3.1 models, ranked first, with month-on-month growth surging 14.8-fold and corresponding active users rising 28.5-fold. The names at the very front of the global growth ranking are almost all task-oriented products.

Place them together and a simple but important principle appears:

in the GPT-5 era, the more a product resembles a dedicated tool, the more likely it is to leave its name on the growth rankings;

the more it resembles yet another all-purpose gateway, the more likely it is to remain in the shadow of the dominant giants.

3. Domestic dark horses: the Minimax ecosystem, WPS AI, and Pic Copilot capture both in-house demand and small consumer pleasures

On the domestic side, the story in the growth rankings is different again.

In the domestic visits-growth ranking, several types of contender appear:

Tunee AI ranks first, as music generation also surges in China;

MiniMax Open Platform + MiniMax Agent:

the former is a model-training/platform gateway for developers and enterprises, while the latter is a To C intelligent-search product. Both rank highly in visits and active-user growth, showing that a strategy combining platform and application has begun to form its own flywheel in China.

WPS AI: as the AI module of established office software, its visits grew more than 60% month on month;

Pic Copilot, Jianpian, Luban, and other Alibaba-affiliated image-editing/design tools posted steady growth, continuing to validate demand for AI to “handle images for you” in e-commerce operations, design-assistant work, and related scenarios.

Viewed through the domestic active-user growth ranking, the pattern becomes even clearer:

Tunee AI, MiniMax Open Platform, and MiniMax Agent remain near the front;

Baidu Comate (coding assistant), Huixiang (video generation), Immersive Translate, and other tools also fall within the 30%–50% MAU growth range.

These products share two characteristics:

they do not seek to replace ChatGPT, but anchor themselves in a fixed scenario with very high repeat frequency;

they do not build a new website for you to sample, but embed themselves in the toolchain you already use: browser bookmarks, office software, browser extensions, and team workflows.

IV. Watch behavioral changes in the browser, not just model versions

What will the launch of GPT-5.1 bring?

For most end-user Web products, it may mean:

a better general-purpose conversational experience;

continued increases in users' expectations of AI answers;

and general questions being handled more readily by system-level gateways.

Yet our October ranking suggests that these changes deserve closer attention:

for which scenarios are users willing to open one more independent browser tab?

Is it to translate better, edit a clip faster, or let an Agent complete routine tasks?

Which behaviors have moved from “is this fun to try?” to “I cannot do without it”?

For example, some creators have already formed the habit of opening Creati / Tunee every day,

while some programmers are deeply tied to Comate / Toolhouse within their company's unified toolchain. Model upgrades are productivity infrastructure; the distribution of Web traffic is the real vote in this round of AI competition.

This October 2025 AI Web dataset cannot tell you what the landscape will look like three years from now.

It can tell you how users are actually behaving in their browsers right now:

whom they trust, whom they depend on, and for which small task they will deliberately open another webpage.

If I hide the model names and look only at browser-tab histories, does my product have a presence?

If the answer is still no, that is all right.

After all, a model can be upgraded overnight,

but a webpage worth opening every day is always worth crafting patiently.

2.2 Concept Definitions

• Geographic dimension

Overseas AI products: products founded by entrepreneurs or teams not of Chinese heritage and launched primarily for global markets, including but not limited to their home markets.

Domestic AI products: products founded by Chinese-national entrepreneurs or teams and launched primarily for China's domestic market.

Outbound AI products: products founded by entrepreneurs or teams of Chinese heritage but whose primary target markets are overseas, outside mainland China.

• Functional dimension

AI-native applications: applications designed from inception around deep integration of artificial-intelligence technologies and algorithms, whose core value, business processes, or user experience depend entirely on AI. They do not merely use AI to optimize or enhance existing functions; AI is their core component, and without it these applications would cease to exist or lose their fundamental value.

AI-enabled applications: applications that integrate or embed AI into an existing business logic and application framework to enhance current functions or provide entirely new ones. These applications may already have had mature business models and market positioning, but introducing AI can significantly improve efficiency and user experience or create new value.

AI-ecosystem applications: platforms that support, connect, or facilitate exchange among AI technology researchers, application developers, service providers, end users, and others in the AI ecosystem. These applications extend beyond technology to markets, communities, resource sharing, and other dimensions, with the aim of advancing adoption, innovation, and collaboration in AI.

2.3 Metric Definitions

• WEB data metrics

Visits: the total number of visits to a website during a specified period, such as one month, used to measure traffic scale. Pageviews during a continuous active period count as the same session; renewed activity after an interval of more than 30 minutes, or activity beginning on a new day, is counted as a new visit, providing a comprehensive and precise measure of traffic and visitor activity.

Unique Visitors: the number of distinct IP addresses that visit the target website during a specified period, such as one month. If someone visits a website on multiple days within one month, that person is counted only once.

Subscription revenue (labeled ARR in the source): all revenue earned over a given period, such as one year, from subscription services provided by the website, excluding one-off sources such as advertising revenue, transaction commissions, and professional services.

• APP data metrics

Downloads: the number of times an App is downloaded during a specified period, such as one month, generally measured as the number of downloads of an individual App from stores such as the App Store and Google Play. Downloads measure an App's popularity and ability to attract users and can also reflect the effectiveness of promotion and marketing.

Active Users: the number of distinct users who performed at least one activity during a specified period, such as one month. Active users measure user scale and engagement during a given period.

In-app purchases (IAP): revenue generated when users buy virtual goods, additional services, premium features, and other items inside an App. This excludes advertising revenue, direct user payments such as tips, and third-party Android app stores.

Appendix: Summary of Quarterly Trend Insights

At the top layer is the entrenchment of gateways. The general conversational gateway represented by ChatGPT has become the global default, while the Chinese market is rapidly consolidating around deepseek, Doubao, Quark, Baidu AI Search, Kimi, and a few others. Users are not looking for the next ChatGPT; they are committing their limited attention to a very small number of brands. This means that the barrier to creating another general-purpose gateway at the level of a browser start page has shifted from a technology problem to one of recognition and habit.

The middle layer is the distribution of tasks. From Creati and Tunee to Toolhouse and Supermemory AI, and then to WPS AI, AI image tools, and translation tools in China, the fastest-growing products share one trait: they do not try to do everything, but make one concrete task something users cannot do without. Once general-purpose models such as GPT-5.1 become infrastructure, real incremental value comes from whoever can better handle a high-frequency action—editing a video, adding music, writing a document, or running an automated workflow.

The bottom layer is the flowering of use cases. In China, Chinese teams are competing more heavily for the default gateway to the Chinese-language world; overseas, they have produced products with an entirely different character. Outbound applications built around AI art, emotional companionship, and creator communities capture narrow openings in culture and demand rather than competing with global giants on parameters and models. Beneath the modest contraction in domestic traffic is the rapid concentration of user behavior around a few leaders and clear use cases; the small universe represented by that 2% outbound share proves that focusing on one scenario and telling its story well can still open a path into the global rankings.

If the AI Web trend in October had to be summarized in one sentence, it would be this: models are becoming homogeneous and gateways are solidifying, yet users' specific tasks, emotions, and habits are continually being reinvented. What is really worth pursuing is not the next giant gateway, but the small use case for which users quietly open one more browser tab every day.
